name: Narmada Udgam Temple, Amarkantak
significance: The principal temple of the pilgrim town of Amarkantak, enclosing the kund accepted as the source of the Narmada. It was raised by the Kalachuris of Tripuri and later renovated by the Holkar queen Ahilyabai.
story: Adi Shankaracharya is said to have declared this stream the true source of the Narmada while searching for its origin.

name: Ahilyeshwar Temple and Maheshwar Ghats
significance: Maheshwar was the Narmada-bank capital of the Holkar queen Ahilyabai, who endowed the town with temples, a fort-palace and the broad stone ghats that still define its riverfront.

name: Kundalpur Jain Temples
style: Square shrines with domed roofs and pinnacles
significance: A Digambar Jain pilgrimage complex of roughly fifty temples on and around a hill northeast of Damoh, centred on the colossal Rishabhanatha image known as Bade Baba. The shrine was renovated around 1700 with help from the Bundela ruler Chhatrasal.
story: Jain tradition holds that Shridhar Kevali, the last of the omniscient ones, attained liberation here.

name: Bawangaja
style: Monolithic Kayotsarga colossus in brown stone
significance: A Digambar Jain pilgrimage centre in the Satpura range of south-western Madhya Pradesh whose 84-foot rock-cut standing image of Rishabhadeva is among the largest monolithic Jain statues in the world, set among a group of eleven temples.
story: Indrajit, Kumbhakarna and other ascetics are said to have attained emancipation here through self-meditation, and their ancient footprint images are preserved at the Chulgiri shrine.

name: Maladevi Temple, Gyaraspur
significance: The largest and finest surviving temple at Gyaraspur, cut partly into the hillside and dedicated to Adinatha, with a dense sculptural programme of tirthankaras, yakshas and yakshis and a foundation inscription of the reign of Valleka.

name: Pashupatinath Temple, Mandsaur
style: Western school of early Indian art
significance: A Shiva temple at Mandsaur, ancient Dashapura, housing a rare 4.5 m eight-faced linga of about the early 6th century that names eight aspects of Shiva. Inscriptions of 404–487 CE record Gupta kings and local donors including silk weavers from Gujarat.

name: Bhoramdeo Temple
significance: A group of four Shiva temples in Kabirdham district whose 11th-century stone temple is covered in figural and erotic sculpture, earning it the name 'the Khajuraho of Chhattisgarh'. Its brick shrine is far older, and the complex was added to between the 7th and 12th centuries.
story: Local lore says the Gond people of the area worshipped Shiva as Bhoramdeo, and that a Naga chief raised the temple.

name: Rajiv Lochan Temple
significance: A temple of four-armed Vishnu at the confluence town of Rajim, ascribed by inscription to Vilasatunga of the Nala dynasty and dated on palaeographic grounds to the 8th century. It is celebrated for its carved doorways and pillars and for the annual Rajim mela.
story: One legend says king Ratnakar built the temple after Vishnu appeared before him as the lotus-eyed Rajiva-Lochana; another that the mythical king Jagat Pal raised it in a single day.

name: Lakshmana Temple, Sirpur
style: Brick temple on a stone jagati with carved stone sanctum doorway
significance: The earliest dated monument at Sirpur, a brick Vishnu temple of about 600 CE whose stone doorway carries Anantasayana Vishnu, the ten avatars and scenes of daily life, and which set a pattern for later building in the Mahanadi valley.

name: Mahamaya Temple, Ratanpur
significance: A goddess temple at the old Kalachuri capital of Ratanpur, counted among the fifty-two Shakti Peethas and revered as Kosaleswari, presiding deity of ancient Dakshina Kosala and family deity of the Ratanpur rulers.
story: Tradition says the temple stands where king Ratnadeva was granted a vision of the goddess.

name: Rajarani Temple
significance: An 11th-century Kalinga temple in Bhubaneswar with an 18 m clustered spire and some of the finest figure sculpture in Odisha; its empty sanctum means it is kept as a monument rather than a working shrine, and its design influenced later central Indian temples.
story: Local belief derives the name from the Naga and Nagini figures at the entrance, read as a king and queen.

name: Brahmeswara Temple
significance: A Shiva temple with four subsidiary shrines, richly carved inside and out, recorded by inscription as the foundation of the Somavamshi queen Kolavati Devi in the eighteenth regnal year of Udyotakesari.

name: Ananta Vasudeva Temple
significance: The principal Vaishnava temple of old Bhubaneswar, founded in the 13th century by the Eastern Ganga princess Chandrika Devi and unusual in worshipping Krishna, Balarama and Subhadra as complete stone images.

name: Dhauli Shanti Stupa
significance: A white peace pagoda on Dhauli hill above the Daya river, built by the Japan Buddha Sangha and the Kalinga Nippon Buddha Sangha beside Ashoka's rock edicts, at a site long central to Odisha's Buddhist heritage.
story: The hill is widely believed to be where the Kalinga War was fought, the carnage that turned Ashoka to Buddhism.

name: Ratnagiri Mahavihara
builtDisplay: 5th–13th c.; main phase under the Bhauma-Karas
style: Post-Gupta brick with chlorite and khondalite carving
significance: A ruined mahavihara on a hill between the Brahmani and Birupa rivers, the major Buddhist monastery of Odisha and a centre of Tantric and Vajrayana practice, with three main monuments, over seven hundred votive stupas and colossal Buddha heads recovered by excavation.
story: Villagers long took the mounds for the palace of a mythical king and called the site the queen's mound.

name: Udayagiri Buddhist Complex
style: Brick and stone stupas, viharas and chaitya-grihas
significance: The largest Buddhist complex in Odisha, known from inscriptions as Madhavapura Mahavihara, forming with Lalitgiri and Ratnagiri the 'Diamond Triangle' of Odishan Buddhism.

name: Lalitgiri
style: Apsidal brick chaitya-griha; Gandhara and Mathura influence
significance: The oldest Buddhist site in Odisha and part of the Diamond Triangle, with an apsidal chaitya-griha, four monasteries and a stupa that yielded relic caskets, showing occupation from the 3rd century BCE through the Tantric period.
story: The site was once identified with the Pushpagiri Vihara described by Xuanzang, though excavation later placed Pushpagiri at Langudi hill.

name: Biraja Temple
significance: The principal temple of Jajpur and a Shakti Peetha, housing a two-armed Durga slaying Mahishasura; it gives the town its names Viraja Kshetra and Viraja Pitha.
story: The Tantra Chudamani says Sati's navel fell here in the Utkala country.

name: Tara Tarini Temple
significance: A hilltop shrine of the twin goddesses Tara and Tarini on the Kumari hills above the Rushikulya river, counted among the four principal Adi Shakti Pithas of India.
story: It is said to mark the place where Sati's breasts fell.

name: Samaleswari Temple
style: Sandhara order, with a pillared circumambulatory gallery
significance: The presiding goddess temple of Sambalpur on the bank of the Mahanadi, whose square sanctum is ringed by a covered pillared passage; it is the leading pilgrimage centre of western Odisha and the neighbouring parts of Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand.

name: Sakshi Gopal Temple
significance: A medieval Krishna temple between Puri and Bhubaneswar, counted among the sixteen Krishna shrines traditionally ascribed to king Vajranabha; it is known for the Anla Navami festival and for offering wheat-based rather than rice prasada.
story: Krishna is said to have walked from Vrindavan to stand witness to a promise made to a poor young man, turning to stone when the youth looked back to check that the god was following.

name: Nrusinghanath Temple
significance: A 45-foot Kalinga-style temple at the foot of the Gandhamardan hills in western Odisha, built by Baijal Singh Dev of Patna State, where Vishnu is worshipped in the rare feline form of Marjara Kesari.
story: The deity is said to have taken cat form to chase the demon-mouse Musika Daitya into a tunnel beneath the hill, and to guard it still.

name: Mundeshwari Temple
builtDisplay: 6th–7th c.; ASI dates it to 108 CE
significance: A hilltop temple on the Kaimur plateau claimed by the Archaeological Survey of India as one of the oldest continuously worshipped Hindu temples in the country, and the earliest surviving Nagara-style shrine in Bihar, unusual for its octagonal plan.
story: Xuanzang is said to have described a hilltop shrine flashing with light in this area during his travels of 636–638 CE.

name: Jal Mandir, Pawapuri
style: Marble water temple in a lotus tank
significance: A white marble Jain temple standing in the middle of a lotus tank at Pawapuri, built on the spot traditionally identified as the cremation place of Mahavira, who attained nirvana here.
story: The fish of the tank are said to wear gold nose rings, and catching or harming them is forbidden.

name: Vishwa Shanti Stupa, Rajgir
significance: A 120-foot white peace pagoda on Ratnagiri hill at Rajgir, founded by Nichidatsu Fujii and completed in 1969, carrying four gilded Buddha statues for four events of the Buddha's life; it is one of some eighty peace pagodas built worldwide by Nipponzan Myohoji.

name: Relic Stupa and Ashokan Pillar, Vaishali
style: Brick stupa; polished sandstone pillar with lion capital
significance: At Vaishali the Licchavis enshrined one of the eight shares of the Buddha's relics in a brick stupa, among the earliest archaeologically known; nearby at Kolhua stands one of the best-preserved Ashokan pillars, 11 m tall and topped by a single lion.
story: Tradition says the Buddha gave the Licchavis his alms bowl here and conjured the illusion of a river in spate to turn them back.

name: Kesaria Stupa
builtDisplay: present structure Pala, 8th–12th c.; origin c. 250 BCE
significance: One of the tallest and largest Buddhist stupas in India, a terraced mandala-form mound about 32 m high whose visible fabric is of the Pala period over a core attributed to Ashoka; its plan invites comparison with Borobudur.
story: Local tradition connects the stupa with the alms bowl the Buddha gave the Licchavis of Vaishali.

name: Shikharji
builtDisplay: present temples 1768 (Jagat Seth); shrines from the 14th c.
style: Hilltop tonks with marble footprint shrines
significance: The most important Jain tirtha, a 1,365 m hill in Giridih district where twenty of the twenty-four tirthankaras are believed to have attained moksha; its summit shrines are held equally sacred by Digambara and Svetambara Jains.
story: Parshvanatha is said to have attained liberation at the Suvarnabhadra kuta, whose footprint shrine is marked by a chatra.

name: Chhinnamasta Temple, Rajrappa
significance: A tantric shrine of the headless goddess Chhinnamasta at Rajrappa in Ramgarh district, drawing two to three thousand pilgrims a day and known for its distinctive tantric design and animal sacrifice.
story: The goddess is shown standing on the bodies of Kamadeva and Rati on a bed of lotus.

name: Maluti Temples
deity: Moulakshi (Mauliksha), with Shiva, Durga, Kali and Vishnu shrines
significance: A village holding 72 surviving terracotta temples of an original 108, built by the Baj Basanta rajas between the 17th and 19th centuries; the Global Heritage Fund has listed them among the world's most endangered cultural heritage sites.
story: The family goddess Mauliksha is said to be the elder sister of the goddess Tara of Tarapith.

name: Tarapith Temple
significance: A tantric temple of the goddess Tara in Birbhum district with an adjoining cremation ground, revered as a mahapitha and among the busiest pilgrimage sites in West Bengal.
story: The temple is inseparable from the tantric saint Bamakhepa, who worshipped here and lived in the cremation ground beside the Dwarka river.

name: Taraknath Temple, Tarakeswar
significance: An 18th-century atchala Shiva temple in Hooghly district housing a swayambhu linga, one of the busiest Shaiva pilgrimage sites in West Bengal, especially at Shivaratri and the Gajan festival.
story: Local legend says Raja Bharamalla Rao built the temple after a linga was discovered in the nearby jungle.

name: Temple of the Vedic Planetarium, Mayapur
deity: Radha Madhava, with the Pancha Tattva and Narasimha
style: Modern temple with a large dome and Vedic cosmological interior
significance: ISKCON's flagship temple at Mayapur, under construction since 2009 and chaired by Alfred Ford, built around a planetarium presenting Vedic cosmology and intended to serve as the movement's global headquarters.
story: Bhaktivinoda Thakur identified this spot in 1894 as the true birthplace of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu.

name: Hangseshwari Temple
style: Ratna temple with thirteen lotus-bud spires
significance: A five-storeyed ratna temple at Bansberia whose thirteen spires and internal plan were conceived around tantric ideas of the channels of the subtle body. Begun by Raja Nrisinhadeb Roy in 1799, it was completed by his widow Rani Sankari in 1814.
story: The deity is named for Rani Hanseswari, the raja's mother, venerated as a manifestation of Kali.

name: 108 Shiva Temples, Kalna
significance: Also called Nabakailash, a complex of 108 Shiva temples at Ambika Kalna set in two concentric circles of 74 and 34 shrines, built in 1809 by the Maharajas of Bardhaman and planned so that every linga is visible from the centre.

name: Jalpesh Temple
deity: Shiva as Jalpesh, Bhairava of the Bhramari Shakti Pitha
dynasty: Koch of Cooch Behar; Raikats of Baikunthapur
significance: A Shiva temple on the Jarda river near Maynaguri housing the linga called Anadi, founded by Bishwa Singha and rebuilt by Raja Pran Narayan in 1653. Its Shivratri fair is among the oldest in northern West Bengal and draws pilgrims from neighbouring countries.

name: Yiga Choeling (Ghum) Monastery
significance: The best known of the Ghum monasteries near Darjeeling, a Gelug foundation of 1875 housing a 4.6 m Maitreya Buddha and 108 volumes of the Kangyur, and a refuge for Tibetan monks since 1959.

name: Parsurameswara Temple
style: Early Kalinga Nagara, with vimana and jagamohana
significance: The best preserved specimen of an early Odia temple, raised in the mid-7th century by the Shailodbhavas, whose family deity was Shiva. It was the first here to set a jagamohana in front of the sanctum, a plan that every later Kalinga temple followed.
story: The temple's name is traced to the penance of Parashurama and the grace Shiva granted him.

name: Chausathi Yogini Temple, Hirapur
deity: The sixty-four yoginis, with Kali at the centre
significance: A roofless circular shrine some 25 feet across, built in 864 CE by the Bhauma-Kara queen Hiradevi, its inner wall set with niches for sixty-four yoginis around a central Kali. It is the earliest of India's yogini temples and the model for those that followed.
story: Priests relate that Durga took sixty-four forms to defeat a demon, and that the victorious yoginis asked to be remembered in a temple of this shape.

name: Sonagiri Jain Temples
style: White hilltop temples with tall spires and a 43-foot manastambha
significance: A Digambar Jain tirtha of 103 temples across a 132-acre hill site near Datia, centred on an 11-foot image of Chandraprabhu known as Bade Baba; the temples date from the 9th century onwards over a much older rock-cut image.
story: Jain tradition holds that since the time of Chandraprabhu five and a half crore ascetics have attained moksha here, among them king Nanganang and half a million followers.

name: Griddhakuta (Vulture Peak)
builtDisplay: associated with the Buddha's lifetime; structures undated
significance: A hill above Rajgir, ancient Rajagaha, that was the Buddha's favourite retreat and the setting given for major discourses including the Heart Sutra, the Lotus Sutra and much of the Prajnaparamita literature. Its name comes from a profile said to resemble a sitting vulture with folded wings.
story: In the Lotus Sutra the Buddha declares that through countless eons he has always lived on Holy Eagle Peak.
